subtopic: STATEMENT ON REDUCTION IN EXCHANGE VALUE OF STERLING

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REDUCTION IN EXCHANGE VALUE OF STERLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as members of the house will be aware the chancellor of the exchequer announced on November 18 the decision of the British government to change the exchange value of sterling from $2.80 (U.S.) to $2.40 (U.S.), a decision which resulted from special circumstances affecting that currency. In accordance with accepted procedures this change in the exchange value of sterling was made with the knowledge and concurrence of the International Monetary Fund. It was accompanied by the announcement of a number of internal measures designed to make ample resources available for improving the balance of payments and ensuring improvement in the competitive position of Britain.
Given the present day pattern of Canadian international trade and payments, this British action will not have a substantial effect on Canada's international financial position. I stated publicly following the British announcement, and would re-emphasize here, that the government of Canada regards the present exchange parity of the Canadian dollar in terms of the United States dollar, that is, $1 Canadian equals 92J cents (U.S.), as appropriate and it intends to maintain this rate.
The Canadian government expects to participate in any support provided through the International Monetary Fund, and the Bank of Canada is taking part in important arrangements being made in co-operation with the central banks of other countries. The total of central bank credit arrangements and the support requested of the International Monetary Fund is massive, and I am confident of its adequacy to ensure the position of sterling at its present rate.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, it is reassuring to have the statement of the Minister of Finance that the devaluation of the pound will not have any financial consequences of great significance for Canada. I am sure all those in the official opposition approve of the support the government of Canada is extending to the pound in these circumstances and to the government of Cape Breton-of Great Britain; Mr. Speaker, I confused two great nations there for a moment.
Devaluation, of course, is the result of a long and difficult period in Britain. I am sure it was not undertaken lightly. I do not propose to make any extensive comments on this occasion, of course the minister must be aware that he has left unanswered a good many questions relating to the increase in competition that this will mean for many of our Canadian industries, both primary and secondary. There will be questions about the effect of this on our prospects for sales of wheat, and whether this will have any effect on our prospects for a world wheat agreement.
Obviously this increases competition generally for our manufacturers, and increases the already urgent need for greater efforts in the area of productivity and an increased effort on our part to cope with inflation. Also there may be some questions as to why the bank rate in Canada was increased 1 percentage point as against half of one percentage point in the United States.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, there are questions on which we and the Canadian people will be seeking information, but as I have said it is reassuring to have the statement of the Minister of Finance that devaluation of the

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to address a question to the Minister of Finance but in view of his statement I can deal better with the matter now. I must say at the outset, sir, that many in different parts of the country with whom I have been in telephone communication this morning do not share the confidence of the minister that the devaluation of the pound will have minimum effects on the Canadian economy.
It may be that these misgivings are shared by the chartered banks, or it may be that the chartered banks are engaged in a bit of a racket, because information came to me this morning that at least one of our chartered banks has issued instructions to its branches to make charges, in the exchange of Canadian for United States funds, in excess of the allowable 1 per cent over the pegged rate. This morning that particular bank charged 91 per cent, and since then an officer of that bank has informed me that they have received instructions from their main office to increase the charge to 10 per cent.
The question I intended to ask was, what is the implication of this action on the part of the banks. Does it mean that the Canadian dollar is becoming unpegged almost inadvertently, or does it mean that the banks are taking advantage of the uncertainty created by the devaluation of the pound, an uncertainty that is understandable in the sterling area but not understandable in the relationship between the Canadian and the United States dollars? Does it mean that they are merely taking advantage of this to make unjustified charges to their customers, and is the minister going to do something about it; because it is bound to have a profound effect on our financial arrangements.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT ON MEETINGS WITH PROVINCIAL FINANCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to questions on Friday last the Prime Minister indicated that I would present to the house today a report concerning the meetings we had last Thursday and Friday with the provincial ministers of finance and treasurers. The president of the Treasury Board, the Minister without Portfolio and myself represented the federal government.
The main purpose of these meetings, as was indicated in my letter of October 24 to the provincial ministers, copies of which were tabled in the house on November 1, was to examine the economic and financial situation and to consider its bearing on the financial policies of the federal and provincial governments. It was not our objective to seek agreement on a specific program of action. Given the responsibility of each minister to his cabinet colleagues and to his legislature or parliament, it would have been inappropriate for any of us to have presented or to have committed himself to financial policies which had not first been presented to his legislature or to parliament.
Our intention in calling this meeting was to enable ministers who have a responsibility for economic and budgetary matters in Canada to examine and exchange views upon the economic and financial situation in the country, and to consider together the direction of fiscal policy which seemed to be called for. I hoped that each minister would feel able to
November 20, 19G7	COMMONS
comment upon the economic and budgetary position of his province, and that all of us would feel free to comment upon any problem which had a particular bearing upon the situation. These expectations were realized in what I believe was an entirely satisfactory meeting.
With the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to table a copy of the agenda which was agreed to and certain tables of financial information provided to the provincial ministers.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT ON MEETINGS WITH PROVINCIAL FINANCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some comments on the statement of the minister and the conference that was held between the minister and members of the government and the ministers of finance of the provinces last week. As I understood the minister's previous statement, part of the emphasis was to be on encouraging restraint and reducing the demands on the capital market. Of course it would be pretty difficult for this to have much effect, in any event, on the premiers of the provinces for the balance of this fiscal year because they would already have made their commitments. In any event I see nothing in the budget speech of the minister of last spring which indicates any particular recognition of the need for restraint. Indeed, he indicated at that time that the economy was in a state of rather delicate balance and that because of this the government was taking off some of the restraints on its own public works programs.
The provinces, of course, have great financial responsibilities in meeting problems in respect of education and so on. While they are struggling with these problems the minister has invited them to meet with him, and I presume he exhorted restraint and moderation while at the same time he knows that the government of Canada, his government, is inviting them actually to expand their expenditures. At the moment I do not intend to make any comment on the merits of the government's program on medicare, but it is
DEBATES	4439
Dominion-Provincial Finance Meetings clear that on the one hand the government is urging the provinces, for the good of the country, to exercise restraint and reduce their demands on the capital market, while on the other hand the same government is inviting them to increase their expenditures by some $1 billion if they all join in, according to the estimates of the minister.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
If the government is convinced that the program should go ahead-and this seems to be on the books and not questioned-this makes a farce of consultation. That is the only point I wish to make. The government should not pretend that this is all a matter of consultation, because a great majority of the provinces representing a great majority of the Canadian people have long expressed their views with regard to priorities. Surely there should be genuine consultation between the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces. We must work -struggle if you like-toward the achievement of an agreement on priorities. We must make sure that the financial resources of the country are placed where they are most urgently needed, and we must rapidly improve the process of consultation. This is dictated not only by the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada but by common sense.
I suggest in all seriousness that this procedure of inviting the provinces to be restrained and cut back on the one hand while at the same time expanding their expenditures obviously may have the effect of greatly increasing spending. This all relates to the believability of the government, and indicates that the government is presenting two faces to the public. Even more serious, this is detrimental to the maintenance and improvement of federal-provincial relations, and will ultimately be destructive of the credibility of the government's intentions and views in respect of the difficulties that have been created in the country with regard to inflation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has not given out very much information as to what proposals he put before the ministers of finance of the provinces. We are not yet aware of what areas of restraint the federal government intends to follow or what areas of curtailment of current or capital expenditures he is asking the provincial governments to enact. I hope the minister will take an early opportunity, either when he brings down his supplementary budget or on the supply
November 20, 1967
4440	COMMONS
Dominion-Provincial Finance Meetings motion, to indicate to the house exactly what the federal government has in mind when it talks about restraints in both current and capital expenditure. I hope he will indicate the order of priorities the government has in mind for itself, and the order of priorities it is seeking to persuade the provinces to accept.
One thing that did come out of the federal-provincial conference of last week with startling clarity was the fact that the Minister of Finance has used that conference to frighten the provincial representatives and the people of Canada out of proceeding with medicare on July 1, 1968. By producing what seems to me to be a highly suspect estimate of the cost he has endeavoured to prevent the provinces from proceeding with the plan to which this government is committed and which this parliament has endorsed.
It is my hope that there will be an early opportunity for us to discuss more fully not only the advisability of proceeding with medicare but the basis of the very dubious estimate which the Minister of Finance has produced regarding its cost to the Canadian people.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT ON MEETINGS WITH PROVINCIAL FINANCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having read over the minister's statement I must agree with previous spokesmen that it does not contain much information. Apparently everything has gone according to schedule, but we do not know what the schedule was, what was contained on the agenda or what were the federal government's plans or intentions. We do not know what the government has in mind in respect of restrictions, or where they should be applied. We do not know what recommendations were made to the provinces as to where they should apply restrictions.
However, I would ask the minister to keep in mind the statements made by some of the provincial representatives after the federal-provincial conference. I refer particularly to the statements by the representative of British Columbia and Mr. Robichaud, premier of New Brunswick. They seemed quite upset in some respects about what the minister had in mind or had proposed at the conference.
We cannot comment much further on the subject because we do not know what transpired at the conference or what was proposed. I hope that some day soon we will find out what happened, and that the minister will take the earliest possible opportunity to inform the house of the proposals made at the conference so we may comment or criticize the minister's actions in this regard.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REPORT ON MEETINGS WITH PROVINCIAL FINANCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in about the same position as other speakers who have taken part in this brief discussion, in view of the fact that the minister has failed to give us any information whatsoever regarding the discussions at the conference. In addition to that, we were given a copy of the minister's statement just after he had begun speaking, so we did not have too much time to give it any consideration following its distribution. We notice that the minister has tabled the agenda of the conference of last week. For some two weeks hon. members of this house have been trying to obtain the details of the agenda so we would at least know what was going to be discussed. However, we were not told, and the agenda has been tabled just today.
We have not been given any information whatsoever on the discussions held or the conclusions arrived at. We have not been told whether there was any agreement between the federal government and the various provincial representatives. Therefore, as far as the whole situation is concerned we are entirely in the dark. Reference has been made today to the statement by the Minister of Finance, his efforts to curtail expenditures, to ease the pressure on the capital market and so on, but it seems to me that very often this government preaches one thing and practises another. We often find that the practice is in opposition to the pronouncements made. It will be interesting to know to what extent the government is prepared to follow the guide lines that have been set out, so the provinces will have at least an appreciation that the federal government intends to do something about this situation.

QUEBEC PREMIER STATEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER NO. 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Quebec premier, Mr. Daniel Johnson, made a major statement over the week-end and I should like, under standing order No. 26 to move, seconded by Mr. Caron from Hull, the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent importance, namely the claim of the Quebec premier who indicated that his government intends to control French language broadcasting and television in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: QUEBEC PREMIER STATEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER NO. 26
speechtext: I doubt very much that the motion of the hon. member is in order; but I believe it would be in order for the house to authorize him to make a few brief comments on the urgency of the debate.

subtopic: QUEBEC PREMIER STATEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER NO. 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can easily see the Speaker's ruling will not be favourable, but nevertheless, briefly and objectively, I will point out the reasons why I think a special and urgent debate should be allowed.
In the whole history of broadcasting in Canada, it is the first time, in my opinion, that the leader of a government makes such a far reaching statement; moreover, there is urgency of debate because it would enable us to look thoroughly into the matter of whether the French language can be better safeguarded by the federal government than by the Quebec government.
An urgent debate could also enable us to consider this afternoon the possibility of the C.B.C. taking action more rapidly as far as the development of French-speaking television in our country is concerned.
It is clear that the problem of Canadian unity is due to the fact that in some areas of our country the French fact is a foreign phenomenon.
November 20, 1967

The urgency of debate arises also from the fact that we could discuss at length the following matter: if the Quebec government exercises its control over the C.B.C., it is possible that the French fact will be limited to Quebec and will not go beyond the borders of Quebec.
And since you will bring up the following argument, namely that the bill is referred to the committee, I will conclude by saying that Bill No. C-163 which is under consideration by the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, deals with the administrative structure of the C.B.C. and not with the French fact, which is urgent, and which the federal government must promote without delay.

subtopic: QUEBEC PREMIER STATEMENT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER NO. 26

Mr. Speaker, the change of 1 per cent in the bank rate was made by the Bank of Canada after consultation with me. It is related, of course, to the action of the Bank of England in raising their rate from 6J per cent to 8 per cent. At the same time the rediscount rate of federal reserve banks in the United States was increased one half of 1 per cent. As the house may or may not know, there is a difference between the operations of the rediscount rate in the United States and the bank rate in Canada. For example, recently the rate on treasury bills in the United States has been well above the rediscount rate in the United States because of the way their facilities are operated.
Here in Canada such a situation is impossible because under those circumstances a bank could go to the Bank of Canada, borrow money to buy treasury bills and make a profit out of it. Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I think I should begin by saying that while I shall have some critical things to say about the government in the course of my remarks this afternoon, I understand that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is travelling across the ocean later today on official business and I should like to say at the outset we wish him bon voyage and a safe trip; of course, I also add that we cannot give him any guarantee at this time that his government will be here on his return.

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Perhaps I might thank my hon. friend for his good wishes and tell him it might be better if I remained here until tomorrow night at eight o'clock so that I could disprove his dire prediction.

I simply wish to make it clear that we are not issuing any guarantee concerning the continued existence of the government or in respect of what his colleagues might do in his absence.
To be a little more serious, Mr. Speaker- although of course I was quite serious in my good wishes to my right hon. friend-this is the first opportunity I have had to make a speech on a government measure as the Leader of the Opposition. I believe the house is entitled to hear from me as one of its officers concerning the attitude and approach of my colleagues and myself to parliament today and to parliamentary business. This I intend to do now very briefly but nevertheless also clearly, I hope, with the indulgence of the house.
I come here with a respect and affection for legislatures, parliaments and parliamentary institutions. I had the good fortune to serve for 18 years in another legislature, first as leader of the opposition and then as leader of the government. I should like to say that I take and took the one responsibility as seriously as the other. A familiarity with legislative and parliamentary traditions and practices bred in me a healthy respect for the potential of parliamentary institutions and for their relevance to modern conditions even after 700 years and as well, sir, a realistic attitude toward the limitations of parliament.
Like most Canadians I have followed the affairs of this house with a great deal of
November 20. 1967

interest but from some distance. So my perspective of parliament has been similar to that of most Canadians. I understand their concern about parliament and I might as well make it clear from the beginning that I share that concern. It is one thing for the people to lose confidence in the government as it is manifest they now have, although happily there is a remedy open to the people and their representatives in that regard; but it is quite another thing when people begin to lose confidence in parliament or in the capacity of parliament to give leadership to the country in dealing with the country's outstanding problems. Such an erosion of confidence would engender frustration, bitterness and in the end despair. Once the people were to lose confidence in parliament they would begin to lose confidence in their country and in themselves. If this were to happen in this most fortunate of countries in the year 1967 it would be one of the scandals of history.
Outside the house I have already said that we intend to be a strong opposition because there is much to oppose in the conduct of this government. There are questions to be asked and explanations to be given which have not been forthcoming, at least in the manner expected by or to the satisfaction of the people of this country. Not only do I say that we wish to be a strong opposition; I say that the present circumstances of this country require an unusually strong opposition, because the weaker the government the greater the need for a strong and informed opposition. But to be strong is not to be obstructive. As I said before, we are in politics to help get things started, not to get them stopped.
If I may speak from a partisan point of view for a moment-I have been speaking generally from the point of view of the public at large-I should like to say that I have no fear of allowing the government to proceed with its legislation. I say to the government through you, sir, let them bring in their program to deal with the present and future requirements of Canada. We will examine that program fully, vote on it in due course and then the people will judge it. I have no political fear of their program because I say to them in as kindly a manner as possible that we have a pretty realistic opinion of their capacity in this regard. Sooner or later they will have to go to the country to defend what they have and have not done. I suppose they will have recourse to that most hackneyed of government election strategies, that
4459
Suggested Economic Mismanagement is, to blame the official opposition for their failures.
We intend to see that the government is judged on its record, on whatever capacity it has demonstrated to deal with the problems of the country and of course, on the other hand, on the strength of the other alternative that is available. This is a comparison and contrast which we on this side of the house look forward to. In the meantime, however, we want parliament to work. I hasten to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not set myself up as an expert on parliamentary procedure, but we want parliament to work as effectively as it can, realizing of course that it will barely work at all unless good leadership is given to the house by the government.
I should like to make two points in this regard. First, I am not convinced that the most appropriate way for parliament to work is to burden this place with dozens of new rules to cover every possible eventuality. It seems to me there is a real danger that a parliament which is subject to excessive or detailed regulations will lose the flexibility and freedom that may be needed to deal with important issues and with the unfortunate crises which do arise from time to time. Therefore I much prefer that we expedite the business of the house by a consensus of the parties rather than by excessive regulation.
Second, I should like to emphasize that any reform of parliament must be such that it will make government more responsible and more responsive to the house, not less, and will make this responsibility more meaningful. Some of the procedures here may be irrelevant. If that is so, let us discard them. But parliament itself is certainly not irrelevant. We should not water down the basic rights of parliament simply because of their antiquity. In looking at the problems which government and parliament must deal with today, I am convinced that some of these old principles, particularly those relating to the accountability and responsibility of government to parliament, are even more necessary under today's conditions than they have been perhaps at any time during the 700 year history of parliament.
The work before us surely is to find procedures that will make these principles more meaningful and will improve their application to modern problems. I am in favour of confining debate on legislation to that which is necessary in respect of the principle and for scrutiny c 1 the details of bills, but believe
November 20, 1967

Suggested Economic Mismanagement that this must be done through agreement among the parties. I believe we might also consider whether it would be advisable to dust off the rules of relevance and repetition which have been enforced more strictly in the British house than in ours. In saying this, sir, I am not implying any criticism of yourself. I also like the hobby-horse of my colleague, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie), which I believe the Prime Minister has been on for some time. We should like to see some more efficient way than we have at present to conduct votes in this house.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Those are examples of what might be desirable with agreement of the parties. The objective, as I say, must be to emphasize the accountability and responsibility of government to parliament and through parliament to the people. Despite the advances and improvements in communications I think the average citizen feels more remote from institutions such as this and from the people who represent him here than formerly, and I sense there is a growing uneasiness in this house on both sides about the difficulty of obtaining a consensus from the public about the great issues of the day.
There are vehicles in parliament for crystallizing issues and for bringing to a head questions of confidence that are in the minds of the people of the country, and ways of making decisions on these in parliament. I think we should use these vehicles, one of which is the supply motion that has now been moved. Surely to debate supply and to demand redress before voting supply is one of the most ancient and basic prerogatives of parliament. I think also it is one of the most relevant to modern conditions, and I intend later on to move an amendment to the supply motion.
There is a definite question of confidence in the government and the conduct of the government which has led us into present difficulties, and a question of confidence in the capacity of this government to resolve them. This question of confidence has been expressed more and more insistently in the press of this country and by the growing uneasiness of investors. It has been expressed by the growing concern and worry of ordinary Canadians going about the daily business of trying to make a living, to provide for their families and to meet rising costs out of their income. There is most certainly a question of confidence, and nothing could be

more clear than the duty of the opposition to raise this and raise it now. Nothing could be more important than that parliament should examine the conduct of this government in the economic field and bring to light the failure of the government and government policies to foster prospects for suitable growth and prosperity equitably shared among Canadians. If parliament cannot discharge this duty and discharge it in a responsible and reasonable way, then surely we are wasting our time here with no sense of a scheme of public priorities and priority problems that Canadians expect us to handle.
It is true that in the course of time we will have a mini-budgetary statement by the minister and at some time a possibility of debating it. If the time comes to vote on that budget we will, of course, vote on the adequacy of the government's budgetary measures. But parliament is also entitled, I suggest, and, indeed, in present circumstances obliged, to examine the government and decide whether on its record it can be entrusted to develop and present measures to deal with economic problems, whether it should be allowed to bring in such a budget and whether the country can stand this government any longer. We must decide in any case, whatever exhortations, forecasts or policies are spelled out by the government, whether the government can any longer be taken seriously. I will return to this matter a little later.
Clearly in this country there is a question of confidence in the government and whether this government, which is in large part responsible for our present economic problems, can be entrusted to solve them. I suggest it is the duty of members of parliament to try to decide this great question of confidence. The indications are surely very strong and clear that the people have substantially less than full confidence in this government, but what must be decided now is whether parliament has confidence.
I want to make it clear immediately that we have great confidence in our society and in the basic strength and future of the Canadian economy. We in Canada have an excellent potential and a strategic position, and there clearly should be no cause for concern about the fundamental capacity of our economy. Having said that I want also to make it clear that I do not minimize the difficulties which confront the government of Canada when dealing with economic matters. I certainly do not minimize those difficulties. But the normal, and I emphasize the word
November 20, 1967

"normal", problems of the Canadian economy as a whole are neither drastic nor disruptive.
From time to time, of course, as we all know, there are local and regional disruptions which are very important and sometimes disastrous to the regions affected. It is unusual, however, for the whole economy of Canada to be subject to sudden heaves and shifts. The normal problems of the Canadian economy, at least in the world context, I suggest are more moderate than severe. They are more or less predictable, or at least the Economic Council of Canada considers them to be so. It has made some predictions and recommendations.
It is my belief that ordinarily the economy will respond to the steadying influence of consistent government policy and reasonable planning, if these are brought to bear at the right time. So that in terms of our natural capacity to grow and sustain our growth, surely we are one of the most fortunate nations of the world. Good fortune, of course, requires good management, and government policies can improve the performance of an economy and they can impede that performance.
We have no desire at all to contribute to the decline in confidence that seems to be growing in Canada or, to put it more accurately, the decline in confidence that seems to be growing among the Canadian people. We want to try to arrest the decline in public confidence, and the most effective and direct way in which that goal can be accomplished, so far as we know, is to try to remove this government.
What is the outlook for the economy? The government has frequently been warned about the prospect of a levelling off or softening of the economy. Indeed, I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) referred to this possibility in the course of making his budgetary speech last spring. That prospect has now become more threatening because of continuing inflation and the growing lack of confidence in this government. We have inflation but we have idle resources in the form of increasing unemployment.
There is no need for me this afternoon to try to place on the record all the indicators as to where our economy is going. I do not think anybody, including the minister, would dispute that the elements are there and that there is already a perceptible slowing down in the economy. The minister might possibly be a little more selective in his statistics so I shall just make one or two references to underline my point.

Suggested Economic Mismanagement
The Economic Council of Canada asserted that a 5 per cent growth rate in Canada for the period 1965-1970 was not only reasonable but would be necessary if we were to develop the employment opportunities required in view of the rapid growth of our work force. Our growth rate in real terms since the spring of 1966, according to the governor of the Bank of Canada, has been hovering between 2 per cent and 2J per cent. This is roughly half the rate of growth that the Economic Council of Canada has said we require.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Let me hasten to say that a levelling off of the economy is not a serious thing if it is temporary. I do not expect the government of the day to be able to maintain everything on a precisely even keel with a growth of precisely 5 per cent per year. But it is not just this flattening out that has to be considered. This slowing down in the growth rate has been going on apparently since the spring of 1966.
Unemployment is now growing. The reasonable target set by the Economic Council of Canada for unemployment is a figure of about 3 per cent. The economic council recommended that it should not be allowed to go above 3 per cent, if possible. By the end of October the rate of unemployment in Canada, seasonally adjusted, was 4.7 per cent. There were 254,000 Canadians unemployed. This represented an increase of about 35,000 unemployed over September and an increase of about 59,000 over the figure for the month of October, 1966. The rate of unemployment is high in British Columbia, the province of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces.
I do not think other indicators offer very much more comfort. One respected financial commentator has reported that there appears to be a 14 per cent decline in the investment intentions in Canada by Canadian subsidiaries of American corporations, and the indications are that private investment intentions generally are also in decline.
So here we have the general story of the economy, a story of inflation accompanied by a slowing down in the growth of our economy. Ordinarily, in conditions of slack the government of Canada should be in a position to consider measures to stimulate the economy, but this government has by its conduct cut itself off these priorities, these options. Increasing unemployment would ordinarily suggest the need to encourage the economy through some such device as a tax
4462	COMMONS
Suggested Economic Mismanagement cut or something else in order to increase the rate of growth and the amount of employment and to cut down the amount of unemployment. Unfortunately, the financial requirements of this government and the inflation toward which the government has contributed so much not only preclude fiscal measures to increase employment but apparently have induced the government to forecast tax increases, which may result in further unemployment.
I do not want anybody to think I am unfair, Mr. Speaker, in attributing a good deal of the blame to the government. Just in case the members of the government did not notice it themselves, I saw a scholarly reference to this subject made by the premier of Saskatchewan in the paper this morning.
Oh, oh.

He said that Canada is threatened by continuing and increasing inflation as well as a soaring cost of living. Then he was quoted as saying:
Our own party-
Which I do not think is the Conservative party.
-as the government, must accept responsibility for the primary blame.
Then he said that the federal government must present policies which will restore responsible fiscal leadership. And so on. I do not just take it upon myself to assess the blame. 1 have been very much influenced by expressions of opinion of that sort.
Hear, hear.

In any case, Mr. Speaker, the government is certainly caught in a box of its own making. Unfortunately, the people of Canada are also caught, against their will and despite the warnings. Perhaps I might quote the following from the Montreal Star of November 17:
We are in for a new and unpleasant experience- inflation, high interest rates and growing unemployment. Until very recently, it was thought impossible to combine these three elements in a single situation.
This government has managed to do it. So we have both inflation and unemployment, and the government seems unable now to work on one problem without making the other worse. But the most tragic fact is that the heaviest burden of all this government's mismanagement falls on those Canadians who can the least afford to bear it. Canadians on low and fixed incomes are usually the first

DEBATES	November 20, 1967
to feel the burden of unemployment and to be the victims of unemployment. They are usually the worst victims of inflation. This burden, as well as being unnecessary, is also profoundly unjust because of all the groups in this wealthy land the ones who most require the assistance of organized society are those who are either very near or even below the minimum margins that are acceptable to a decent and a civilized people. In place of help they are suffering the heavy penalty of disorganized and undisciplined government. I do not need to dwell on this matter, Mr. Speaker. The effects of inflation are well known in this house and to the Canadian people.
In the short term inflation, of course, strains the economy by increasing the gap between what people are accustomed to and what they are able to buy under these circumstances. That is serious enough, but I do not propose to dwell this afternoon on the effects of our high cost of living because I believe this subject has been debated previously during this session.
I want to emphasize particularly, important as these other effects may be, the effect of these conditions on our economy, our outlook and our future. In the longer term inflation could strangle the Canadian economy because as prices rise, as production recedes, our capacity to compete in world markets and to sell our goods declines also. Certainly the degree of inflation which has taken place in this country in recent years has seriously undermined our ability to compete and our ability to move ahead at a satisfactory rate.
Hear, hear.

The rate at which prices have been rising in Canada, particularly in the last two or three years, far exceeds the rate in our great neighbour the United States. Not only is it much greater than in the United States but it is more than double the rate of the rise in the price level which the Economic Council of Canada has said is tolerable for this country.
Let me just mention some figures to remind the house. The Economic Council of Canada stated that Canada's economy could perhaps sustain an average annual price rise of something ranging between 1.4 per cent and 2 per cent. In 1963 the rise was within that span; it was 1.8 per cent. In 1964 it was 2.5 per cent. In 1965 it was 2.9 per cent. In 1966 it was 4.6 per cent, and I understand that this year so far it has been 3.6 per cent. These figures are to be compared with what
November 20, 1967	COMMONS
the economic council suggested was tolerable. When you compare them with the comparable figures for the United States you see just what damage has been done to our ability to compete.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
In 1964, for example, the price increase in the United States was 1.6 per cent as against 2.5 per cent in Canada. In 1966 the increase in the United States was 3 per cent as against 4.6 per cent in Canada. It must be emphasized that the United States has been able to do a more effective job than Canada has done in restraining the rate of price increases despite the fact that it has been involved in the war in Viet Nam, virtually a major war. An examination of the differences in the rate of price increases between our country and the United States indicates that we have lost a great part of the competitive advantage which we derived from the devaluation of the Canadian dollar in 1962. This again is not just my opinion. I might remind the house of an analysis appearing in the London Economist of September 30 which reads as follows:
For the past two years, Canada has failed to match that cost and price performance of the United States. The economy has been overloaded, the limits of capacity too closely approached and a wave of cost and price increases generated which continues to sweep through the economic system after the boom has topped out.
This represents an indictment of this government's fiscal policies which certainly cannot be ignored. The same article refers to the minister's policies in these terms:
Mr. Sharp, alas, cannot avoid the responsibility for inadequate fiscal action, the need for which he now seems belatedly to realize.
I think this may be a little unfair to the Minister of Finance, and I am not sure that this has been the real problem in the government. Certainly I do not wish the Minister of Finance to think I am picking on him. My criticism is directed against the government as a whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sensitive.

Besides the need for sensible and systematic budgeting policies, the economic council, and others of course, have recommended other important policies in the fight against inflation. The importance of increasing productivity in Canada has been emphasized as a means of fighting inflation.
I think we all recognize the importance of this and we are all concerned about the apparently dismal performance of Canada
DEBATES	4463
Suggested Economic Mismanagement with reference to productivity. I do not think I need document this. I think it is unquestionably so. Indeed, I understand that Canada has ranked fourteenth among the 14 industrial nations of the western world over a period of time, and I think this is something about which we should all be concerned.
Many factors are involved in this but surely the most important factor associated with the question of productivity is the matter of the technical and vocational skills of our people and the rate at which these are being increased. This of course involves general education, which is a provincial responsibility; it involves vocational and technical training and, speaking generally, it involves an upgrading of skills. The Economic Council of Canada pointed to Canada's rather disappointing performance in this regard over the years and urged us to continue making a greater effort. Until last spring this was a shared responsibility in the field of trades and technical training, with the provinces and the federal government sharing the cost. About a year ago the federal government decided to split rather than share the financial responsibility and it announced that as of April, 1967, it would no longer share in the cost of operating vocational training programs associated with the provincial public school systems. On the other hand, it announced it would assume full responsibility for the vocational training of adults. At the same time the government announced new arrangements with regard to postsecondary education, but I am not concerned with that today.
The provinces were to be consulted before these new arrangements for vocational training were announced. Actually, federal officials made tentative arrangements to visit the provinces for the purpose of consultation but these tentative arrangements never materialized. I do not attribute this to any lack of good intention on the part of those involved. That is pretty specific, and there ought to be no compromise. There are no grounds whatsoever for the fallacious argument of inflationary pressures as a reason for postponing medicare. On the basis of priority surely the health of the Canadian people ought to have a top claim upon government programs and expenditure.
Let me say that in the opinion of members of this party Canada can afford medicare and can afford to start it on July 1, 1968. I do not intend first to tell the government to tighten its belt and stop spending money without indicating where expenditures could be cut. I suggest there are expenditures which the government could curtail and which would pay all the federal government's share of the medicare program without imposing new taxes.
Let us have a list.

First of all, we keep a brigade and air force squadrons in Europe today which may have had a military role to play 20 years ago but are being kept there today largely for political purposes. Some 20 years ago there was a danger of military aggression by the Soviet union and Germany was prostrate and militarily weak. Those conditions no longer obtain. The Canadian government could withdraw these military forces from Europe. It could also discontinue some of the contributions we are making to NORAD which are no longer relevant in light of the technological changes that have taken place in recent years. On those two programs alone the government could save $300 million. It could postpone the refitting of the Bonaventure at a saving of $11,800,000. It could postpone the construction of two support ships which are to cost $49,100,000. It could drop the purchase of 115 CF-5 aircraft, which many consider to be obsolete, at a saving of $215 million. I have already suggested greater savings than it would cost the federal government to carry out medicare in the coming year.
Let me also suggest to the government that it could find tax revenues which it has not even begun to tap at present. We in this party are opposed to an across the board tax increase, first of all because it would impose a burden upon millions of Canadians in the


middle and lower income groups whose standard of living in many cases has already been reduced because of rising costs of living and, second, because this could be the final tipping of the scale which might precipitate an economic recession in this country. If the government requires more revenue it could implement some of the recommendations of the Carter commission report. That commission pointed out very clearly that the middle and lower income groups in Canada have for decades been carrying an unduly heavy share of the tax burden. It also pointed out that for decades in Canada we have had freeloaders who have been getting a free ride and who have by special legislation and special concession, including depletion allowances and depreciation allowances, and because of the absence of a capital gains tax, not been contributing their fair share toward paying for the services rendered by the government of Canada. It has also pointed out that on the basis of 1964 tax returns insurance companies should have paid another $75 million had they been on the same tax base as other corporations. It points out that the extraction industries, the mining and petroleum industries, managed to avoid payment of $152 million that would have been paid by manufacturing companies or other business enterprises.

It points out that by restructuring the Canadian tax system persons with incomes of $5,000 a year or less could have a reduction of 10 per cent in their income tax payments, and those earning between $5,000 and $10,000 a year could have a reduction of 7 per cent. It points out that corporations would be required to pay an additional $532 million, $271 million of which would come from foreign investments.
If the government is going to tell us that it needs more money, and the Minister of Finance told us on motions the other day that it is his intention to raise taxes, I say that before any thought is given to an across the board increase in personal income tax the minister ought to look at some of the freeloaders who have not been paying their share, according to the Carter commission report, and who should now be called upon to carry their fair share of the tax burden of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to this afternoon's debate, and particularly to the address of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), with some nostalgia. My memory went back to the time when I was in London in the spring of 1962, having spent a year studying there with the intention of spending another year away from home. I had left in a bank in Canada the funds to pay for the second year of travel, intending, when the end of the study year came, to withdraw these funds and to change them into British pounds and American dollars to pay for the trip the rest of the way around the world. One morning I opened a newspaper to discover that the Canadian dollar had been devalued in order to cope with the financial crisis that had come about through what I had assumed then, and about which I have

not had reason to change my mind, was the mismanagement of the then Conservative administration in Canada. So it is not surprising that on a day when we are all contemplating the significance of another devaluation, this time of the British pound, even the new Leader of the Opposition should be impatient to get another chance at the control of the Canadian dollar.

speechtext: I hope we can disappoint them again.

I made it home just six days before the election in 1963. One might, I suppose, call my presence here a sequel to the story that I told.
However, I became more optimistic when the Leader of the Opposition spent some time discussing the rules of parliament and expressed a hope that we would see an end to repetitious debate. It struck me that these words might have better been said in caucus than on the floor of the house, and I regretted that he should have rushed into a motion of want of confidence because if his hopes are borne out tomorrow night we will no longer have the opportunity of seeing what he can do about repetition in debate. If in the next six months or so he were able to end that unhappy feature of this institution, I am sure we would have much greater confidence in his ability to solve the financial, economic and other problems of our nation.
My purpose this afternoon is not in any way to bail out the government from the crisis they have brought upon themselves. We in the Social Credit party have been saying for a long time that all is not well with the present monetary system used in this country and around the world. Every time we raise our voices to question the system, we are told that we are the ones who are foolish and who have strange ideas about money, and that all we have to do is sit back and let the system work and everything will be fine. Yet we continue to go from one financial crisis to another no matter how our knowledge of technology and science advances. As a result we feel that we have not been so far wrong through these years.
We have criticized the government for a long time for failing to make available to the public service capital at low rates of interest through the Bank of Canada. Had some of the measures advocated years ago by Social Credit been put into effect, we would not be in such a desperate need for schools, hospitals, sewers and pollution control on which

all levels of the government are now compelled to spend enormous sums of money.
Because the effort was not made earlier and because financing was not directed in the proper places at that time, we are faced now with having to tackle the same problems which we cannot escape in the midst of a financial crisis. We have been concerned through the years about the failure of all administrations at the federal level to tackle the problems of reducing the national debt in order that debt financing should not continue to use up such an enormous portion of the tax revenue that is available to the government each year. While the government does use the Bank of Canada to help to reduce annually service charges on the national debt, in time of prosperity it has not taken the measures that would have used that prosperity to cut back on that drag on federal budgets.
We have said over and over again that taxation has been placed on the wrong areas entirely. Here I feel compelled to speak of the 11 per cent sales tax on construction materials which was ostensibly imposed to raise revenue and, I suppose, to slow down construction, although why one would want to slow down construction at any time in recent years in Canada I do not know. -and this house urges the government to take effective steps to meet this situation by the creation of a Canada Investment Board to set priorities for both public and private investment, by a return to a floating exchange rate and the control of capital movements across our borders, by the immediate implementation of those recommendations of the Carter Commission which call for taxing gains now escaping taxation, and by making it crystal clear that medicare will commence on July 1, 1968.
We contend that the first two or three of those suggestions are answers to the endangered rate of economic growth and the prospects of satisfactory levels of employment. The expenditure programs in the budget this year have been designed to meet many of these requirements and at the same time to provide an expansionary stimulus to the over-all level of economic activity. In other words, Mr. MacNaughton in that speech, and in fact in many of the speeches he made at that time, recommended that we should run a budgetary deficit this year, one that was designed to stimulate the economy, just as the province of Ontario itself ran a substantial deficit this year. Mr. Speaker, I believed this was the kind of budget that was appropr.ate to the circumstances; and I still believe that, and so does the provincial treasurer of Ontario whom I met and talked with the other day.
Our present problem is very different and I hope my hon. friend, as he learns more about the finances of Canada, since I know he mastered so well the finances of Nova Scotia, will begin to understand the nature of the inflationary problem we face. It is not the tradit onal kind of inflationary problem, as I think he understands to some extent because, as I will say subsequently, I agree with many of the things he said in his speech. I would like to make it clear that the kind of inflationary problem we are dealing with is a completely unprecedented one. It is one that is universal, that is international. It exists in other parts of the world as well as here, and it arises out of what I have called, and many people are now calling, an inflationary psychology. It is one of those peculiar situations we have never seen before, when rising interest rates are an accompaniment of easy money policies, and when prices and wages have continued to rise even after some slack developed in the economy. That is our problem. It is to be found in an exaggerated form, of course, in the United Kingdom, and I hope the kind of measures we are taking here will prevent the kind of problems that have arisen there, and have swept the finances of the world.
I say to my hon. friends in the N.D.P. that the kind of policies they are now advocating

I suggest one of the things the government could do would be to organize additional activities for the economic council. Perhaps the structure of it may have to be changed somewhat in order that this could be done, but the economic council could undertake active discussions between governments, management and labour in order to ascertain if something could be done about productivity. The Minister of National Revenue knows full well that manufacturing productivity has been on the decline in Canada for the last three or four years, and in relation to the United States is still about 30 per cent below that country. As long as we have that disparity in manufacturing productivity, then talk about parity of wages, talk about active competition with the United States, is utter nonsense.
We are facing direct economic aggression from countries abroad. They, too, have to survive as a result of the Kennedy round. The governor of the Bank of Canada and the minister himself have been talking about the excessively high wage increases that have been negotiated in 1966, and are still coming about, without any compensating increase in productivity, c (9:20 p.m.)
This is where one of Canada's greatest ills lie. They lie in the declining productivity of

Suggested Economic Mismanagement our industry, which do not match government expenditures. Lord only knows, there are expenditures at every level of government and not just at the federal level. One only has to study the report of the Tax Foundation to see readily that the provinces and municipalities incur their own expenditures in this regard. It might be interesting to look at what Mr. Burns has to say, to illustrate what I have just said. I will use the table of figures that he has included in his article. They are for 1966-7 and 1965-6, in any event, let us look at them. He says:
In 1950, which is a reasonable year for measuring immediate post-war "normalcy", federal nondefence expenditures on goods and services were equal to 2.7% of the gross national product. In the same year, provincial expenditures were 3.0% and municipal 4.6%. But in the current increase in governmental activity it has been the provinces and the municipalities that have exercised their claims. Between 1950 and 1965, the federal share of non-defence expenditure on goods and services rose to 3.3% of the gross national product or by 22%. The provincial percentage rose to 4.3% or by 43% while that of the municipalities went to 7.9% or up by 71%.
If we look at total government expenditure (exclusive of intergovernmental transfers) which rose from 22.1% of the gross national product in 1950 to 31% in 1965, we find that the share of the government of Canada rose from 11.5% to 13.4% or by about 17%. The share of provincial governments went up by 59% from 5.6% to 8.9%. The municipal share increased from 5.0% to 8.7% or about 74%.
The figures in themselves are not important. They are but a reflection of our changing demands-
I terminate my remarks by making a plea to the minister and the administration. First, do something constructive to enable management, labour and government to solve problems of productivity and to bring about greater co-operation between the three levels of society to deal with problems of policy. Such action ought to deal with the problem of parity of wages across the country as well as with all sorts of other things. It would be a step in the right direction in dealing with problems of productivity. Lack of productivity is one of the root causes of inflation.
Second, the government must, of course, show an example by restraining its expenditures. It should not try to fool the country and this house with stories of great cut-backs on estimates which are really puffery. As I said in a speech last week in this house, the government can start with initial estimates of $15 billion and pare those to $11 billion and leave the impression that expenditures are to

be reduced by $4 billion. The government would still end up with $11 billion in expend-iures when, in the previous year, expenditures had run at about $10 billion. There would be no gain.
Last week's conference between the Minister of Finance and provincial representatives was a step in the right direction.

I caution, hon. members and Mr. Speaker, that most decisions of government ought not to be taken at dominion-provincial conferences. That pattern ought not to be set at such conferences, since this house would become a mere rubber stamp. This is the dilemma we face. I agree with what the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon. There must be consultation with the provinces.
I suggest, when we take steps to increase our productivity, that everyone in this country will benefit. We shall compete more effectively abroad than we now do. Incomes will increase and a whole panoply of benefits will accrue to Canada. Ultimately the government will benefit and it will be able to establish on an economically sound basis programs of social justice, which we all want to do our best to provide.
Look at Britain, Mr. Speaker. There is a classical example. For the last 20 years Britain has engaged in activities which have been way beyond her capabilities. One segment of the population believes in fiddling while London burns; another segment is so hidebound in doctrinaire restrictive practices that it cannot see that only if goods are produced will there be employment; they are more interested in tea breaks. Management over there refuses to innovate and refuses to take steps to really compete abroad. The net result has been the morass in which Britain now finds itself. I do not know, but it seems to me that Britain tried to move too fast in certain sectors and had not the economic structure on which to build many of the fancy programs it has. Our tendency, unfortunately, has been to follow Britain down that road. To that extent I feel that there has been mismanagement with regard to the financing of this country. The position we are in today is, certainly, not the result of good management.
November 20, 1967

I will be very brief in my remarks with respect to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). In effect, he urges the government to set certain priorities for public and private investment, to implement the recommendations of the Carter commission immediately, apparently without even studying or assessing their contents, and to give this country a guarantee that medicare will commence on July 1, 1968. Then, consistent with the other socialist recommendations contained in his speech, the hon. member suggests we finance all these things simply by cutting costs; he moves immediately to his favourite theme,
Suggested Economic Mismanagement that we should cut our expenses in connection with NATO, NORAD, refitting naval vessels, the provision of military aircraft and so on. The leader of the New Democratic party, whom my friend from Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Deachman) called "the last of the big spenders", is quick to call for defence cuts of all kinds, notwithstanding the fact that we have an extended defence policy, a smaller force and a budget which is the same as it has been for a number of years in terms of amount, though in terms of buying power it is worth a great deal less-defence has been hit far more by spiralling costs than have most other departments, yet the hon. member now urges us to pull out of our major responsibilities.
Speaking on my own behalf and not on behalf of the government, it is my opinion that having cut 20,000 men off the strength since 1963, and with still further cuts forecast, and with a defence expenditure amounting to 2.8 in terms of the gross national product, a whole percentage point lower than it was, we ought to be very cautious about making further cuts in this area. Our present spending puts us in the same category as Denmark and Luxembourg-at the bottom of the list of NATO nations.
While unification has enabled major economies to take place-it has certainly enabled us to reduce the number of people engaged in the administration without cutting too deeply into our operational forces-and while there are still some savings in store, the real economies already have been achieved; further reductions must be at the expense of bone and muscle. Personally, I hope that when this area of government expenditure is under review we can at least count on the support of the official opposition.

Perhaps it is worth while looking back on the economic events of the past few years. I like the assessment of David W. Slater in the Queen's Quarterly for spring, 1967. The author says that six features of Canadian economic performance during the last decade and a half can be counted as outstanding successes. First, except for a period of four or five years the country had quite an impressive attainment of full employment. The second outstanding success, he tells us, is the full-fledged
November 20, 1967

Suggested Economic Mismanagement Canadian participation in remarkable postwar growth in world trade and output, particularly among the highly developed countries. Third, Canada has been remarkably free from serious persistent deficits or surpluses in her over-all external balance of payments. Later, Dr. Slater writes:
A fourth success has heen Canada's comparatively favourable experience in adapting to a huge expansion of the urban-industrial-commercial-administrative activities of her people. The rates of urban growth in Canada have been extraordinarily high during the last two decades, compared with other industrial countries.
Any serious analysis of the way in which Canadians have been migrating to the larger residential centres would disclose the kind of economic pressures which have been imposed on all concerned, with resulting heavy burdens on both federal and provincial governments.
The fifth success, Dr. Slater says, has been achieved by improving educational activities in Canada, in further reducing inequalities of opportunity and in adapting the social welfare system to a modern industrial-urban society.
Finally-and this is of great importance in our centennial year when we think of our country as a unity-the author states:
The prairies, and now Quebec and perhaps the Atlantic provinces, seem to be full and hopeful participants in the modem economic growth processes. And Canada has worked up some fairly successful mixtures, uniquely adapted to her circumstances, in blending public and private power and public and private enterprise.
I think it is one of the characteristics of the party which I have the honour to support that we have not been doctrinaire. We have been most anxious to harness and stimulate private enterprise and to encourage economic freedom in every way, while at the same time carrying out a wise public policy. We see the government and industry as partners.
Dr. Slater looks at the failures of the past decade and a half, and here he says the greatest failure lies in our inability to reduce the relative shortfall in Canadian productivity, and in the persistence of levels of living below those which prevail in the United States.

The second notable failure, he says- and fortunately this situation now has been corrected-was the high level of unemployment between 1958 and 1962. We hope these conditions will never be repeated.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke about mismanagement, and my mind was immediately attracted to something which was said

by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revel-stoke (Mr. Johnston) who remarked of the hon. gentleman's speech: "He did not look beyond the frontiers of Canada for factors which influence the Canadian economy". I think it is characteristic of the Minister of Finance as well as of his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) and as well, indeed, as of the ministry as a whole, that to a remarkable degree there has been attention paid to the the external forces. John Deutsch recently said:
As more trade barriers are dismantled (and this is the main objective of the Kennedy round), there will be still more chances for industries to specialize and gain the economies of scale.
I would so much like to have heard the Leader of the Opposition, who comes from the maritimes, dilate on this matter which is of such great importance to Canada and its future.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
It is a fact that in many ways President Kennedy's hopes for an Atlantic free trade area have been disappointed. The exclusion of Britain from the common market began a period of increasing doubt and suspicion between the United States and Europe. This suspicion was reflected and aggravated by the tough bargaining attitudes which developed at Geneva. After four years of bargaining, the GATT negotiations and the Kennedy round finally came to a conclusion, which, on a simple arithmetical basis, I think means an average reduction of approximately one third in tariffs between industrial countries throughout the world, spread over the next five years. Despite this failure to reach the 50 per cent this does open up, I think, exciting new possibilities.
Since world war II Canada's greatest achievement economically-and this, is the reason for the comparative success of the last 15 odd years-has been our integration into the expanding world economy. This, has been very much the policy of this government. I hope it is a policy that will be supported in his "in-depth" speech on the mini-budget by the Leader of the Opposition.
Canada has already been an active participant in reconstructing a viable, rational, internationally oriented world economy. We made our contribution at Bretton Woods. We have been active in GATT; and although it has caused some suffering in sectors, Canada has been prepared to make sacrifices to see our economy shift to an international position. Canada has resisted the temptation to
November 20, 1967	COMMONS
retreat to a nationalistic autarchical system. I think there may be a danger that we lose confidence in the attractiveness of an aggressive, outward looking policy. Certainly Canada lost that confidence in the mid-1950's, and this has been commented upon by economists of several western powers.
Some people say that the dominant trend today is not toward a more liberal and expansive economic system, but toward fragmentation. They see a failure on the part of the United States and the United Kingdom to win acceptance of a reformed monetary system. This morning I was listening to a news report. Someone from the United Kingdom was commenting on Britain's huge disappointment with respect to recent attitudes of France in international affairs, in defence arrangements, and particularly in international monetary arrangements. France's failure to assist in an effective scheme for increasing international monetary reserves has placed certain countries of the world, now notably the United Kingdom, on the brink of international monetary collapse. I think that this is the real way, in the middle and long run, that Canada can make a positive contribution to productivity growth, and I think this is a view reflected by the ministry.
I notice that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) in Vancouver on January 18, 1967, said:
One of the most striking features of the past few decades has been the extent to which the interests of nations have become interdependent. We have always, of course, been affected by the actions of others. But now the earlier simple and limited relations between states have given way to a complex and pervasive system of interrelationships which any government ignores at its peril.
No one, I am sure has been more conscious of this than the Minister of Finance. No one has been more active in trying to develop for our country outward looking policies. The limitations to which this is possible depend on many factors outside our frontiers.
The Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), speaking in Montreal on March 1, 1967, said:
We live in an interdependent world-and a world which through technology and communications is becoming more interdependent. We can only live independently, and successfully in that world, by learning to take advantage of the benefits which interdependence offers us.
The Minister of Forestry has his Ph.D. in economics. When we examine this government we can see no shortage of technically qualified economists. There are at least six
