Now, sir, recently we have heard public utterances by Harry Johnson, who left the senior chair in economics at Chicago to assume the senior chair in economics at the London School of Economics. He has spoken of the trend toward regionalism of world trade which bears, as he sees it by definition, a threat to Canada's trading interests. He sees the great problem facing Canadian policy makers as being the problem of safeguarding as much of Canada's trading interests as can be preserved in a fragmenting international economy.
I heard and spoke briefly with Dr. Johnson at Queen's University on May 20, 1967. May I summarize what he said to that convocation gathering-and I believe his advice is something we should bear in mind as we look forward to this challenge of not only increasing productivity but strengthening Canada in the world society. Dr. Johnson said:
Three years ago, X took the position that the world economy stood at a crossroads, with respect to the three major components of international economic organization

the international monetary system, international trading arrangements, and the promotion of the economic growth of the less developed countries.
In the field of international monetary organization, it was clear that the advanced industrial nations of continental Europe were no longer happy to hold United States dollars as international reserves in place of gold, the supply of which commodity had for long failed to grow rapidly enough to satisfy the need for international reserves of a growing international economy.
I seem to remember that the Minister of Finance in one of his addresses to this house, spoke of a danger of growing international illiquidity. Dr. Johnson stated:
In the field of international trade, the formation of the European economic community-the common market-was threatening to divide the western world into regional trading blocs, discriminating against trade with each other and incidentally against the trade of the less developed countries.
Then finally Dr. Johnson concluded with reference to the underdeveloped countries, when he said:
-it was clear.. .that the amount of development aid the developed countries were likely to furnish to the less developed was likely to fall short of what would be required-
Kenneth Galbraith, who has given top level advice to successive American administrations, but who nevertheless remains a very enthusiastic Canadian, discussed in Weekend Magazine of March 25, 1967, the
November 20, 1967

Suggested Economic Mismanagement possibility of wider trading arrangements among our country, Britain and the United States, seeing this as a possible step towards the ideal of an Atlantic community, which through France's attitude is not now possible, but eventually I hope may be. He sees this not as something that will diminish Canada in its influence but as something that is within forseeable possibility, perhaps the policy most clearly designed to increase our gross national product in Canada and to increase the productivity of the individual worker. Weekend magazine carried a report of an interview with Dr. Galbraith, during which he was asked whether there was any real interest in Britain in such a proposal. He replied:
I think there is. There are a substantial number of people in Britain who fear the notion of a little Britain. They don't think it has a future as an "off-shore island"...
My impression is that Professor Franck, who has been in England in recent months, has found quite a few people who are rather anxious to talk about the idea of an Atlantic trading community.
I hope that the Leader of the Opposition, who comes from a part of Canada which I am sure could only benefit from such a development, will lend his full support to this general approach which is calculated to strengthen our economy and preserve our interests.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I see many reasons for encouragement in spite of these disappointments, to which I have referred. I am looking at the Fourth Annual Review of The Canadian Economy From The 1960's To The 1970's published by the Economic Council of Canada in September of this year. It shows the growth and volume of merchandise exports for the period 1950-60 standing at 4.6 per cent. In the period from 1961-63 it is 7.4 per cent. Now, in the period 1963-66 it is shown as 11.1 per cent. Not bad. What about merchandise imports? We see there an increase from the period 1950-60 of 5.2 per cent, dropping down between 1961 and 1963 to 3.3 per cent, but rising dramatically in the period between 1963 and 1966 to 13.8 per cent. Not too bad.
When we look at the employment by regions we find that in 1961 unemployment as a percentage of the labour force is 7.2 per cent. Yet, in 1966 we find it is down to a figure of 3.6 per cent which, some economists tell us, is tantamount to full employment.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) spoke of the Productivity Council. I have searched carefully and I can find no
[Mr. Matheson.J
evidence on my own or from any person's comments that there have been any useful suggestions whatsoever from the deliberations of the Productivity Council. Again he spoke of the declining productivity and I think it is fair to say there has never been a decline in productivity. But there has been less improvement in productivity than increase in wages. Of course, that is a rather disturbing fact. The Economic Council of Canada, which was established in 1963, set up what I regard as manifestly wise objectives which, to a large measure, have already been achieved-full employment, a high rate of economic growth, reasonable stability of prices, a viable balance of payments and an equitable distribution of rising incomes. We need more of the same.
The fact is that by all standards we enjoy one of the highest standards in the world, and it improves dramatically year by year. I have attempted to find current figures for the year 1967, but have been unable to do so. Looking at the record of growth for the economy for the period from 1963-66, however, I find that wages, salaries and supplementary labour income percentages moved from 8.8 in 1963-64 to 11.1 in 1964-65 and to 12.9 in 1965-66. Not bad. I find that personal disposable income percentages increased from 5.7 for the period 1963-64 to 10.3 for the period 1964-65 and to 10 for the period 196566. Very good. When we look at the other side of production we find that profits before taxation for the same three year period are respectively 15.1 per cent, 7.9 per cent and 0.7 per cent.
This is the challenge which faces us. The hon. member for Edmonton West speaks of the financial malaise. I have been looking at the figures published by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and I find that personal consumption expenditures have increased from $25,926 million in 1962 to $35,272 million in 1966, the last period available. The gross national product has increased from $40,575 million in 1962 to $57,740 million in 1966. Even if we take these figures and reduce them to the constant 1957 prices we discover that the increases in expenses of governments at all levels have increased less than the prices for the same period, although not by very much. Prices have increased by 125 per cent. Government expenditures have increased by 123 per cent. We know that the federal government, and I believe other governments as well, are now engaged in a most serious attempt to improve the situation by substantially cutting their own costs.
November 20, 1967

Mr. Speaker, I ask the following question which has been suggested by the motion of the hon. Leader of the Opposition and by the speaker who followed: Are we running out of prosperity? I say categorically that we are not. The employment performance in recent years has been excellent. From the early 1960's to the later 1960's there has been an expansion of one million jobs in Canada. Just how good this is is shown by the fact that this increase in a million jobs in under four years is more than the increase in the whole decade of the 1950's. It is also larger than the increase over the whole 17 years from 1929 to 1946. My authority for this statement is Canadian Business of January, 1967. This publication states:
The projected growth rate of employment is greater in Canada than in all other industrially advanced countries over the medium-term future. The favourable employment outlook also means a rise in real income per capita. This is so because the number of workers will rise in relation to both the younger and older people outside the labour force.
Average annual growth since 1963 has been more than 6% per year in volume of output. There has never been a more prosperous time in Canada. Result has been that this country has moved into the front ranks of economic expansion among industrially advanced nations since 1963.
Canadian exports have reached record levels since 1963. Volume of exports has grown about twice as fast as the volume of total output in this period.
In other words, as I say, we are moving competitively into the international society. There are these dangers about increasing prices and wages and declining profits. We must face this problem collectively, and if we do so wisely the future is very bright. There has been an upsurge in exports of wheat and happily an even more dramatic upsurge in exports of highly manufactured products. We are lucky that our farmers and the needs of the world have contrived to help Canada enormously in these past years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 3 I asked a question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen). Following his reply that he would like to discuss the matter with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and make a reply later, I stated I would like to discuss the matter at ten o'clock.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The point to which I directed my question on November 3 was one which I raised in this house in the month of October of this year having to do with the application of federal funds for hospital operating purposes in the province of Quebec. You may remember that in October I asked a question regarding four hospitals in the province of Quebec about which the affairs of the board of governors had come to my attention during a visit to Montreal. I outlined to the house how these hospitals were months behind in receiving their remittances from the Quebec hospital insurance commission, and that the boards of governors were in desperate straits in trying to meet the financial commitments of the hospitals.
Since I made those comments regarding the four hospitals in Quebec, of which 1 have personal knowledge, I have received the annual report of the Montreal Children's Hospital for the 12 months ending December 31, 1966. Being a member of the Canadian House of Commons I can only ask how our federal funds are being handled, once they are transmitted to the minister of health for Quebec. I assume I am not allowed to ask how the province of Quebec handles the money it presumably directs toward the hospitals in that province, that being a provincial matter.
November 20, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
However, upon reading the report of the Montreal Children's Hospital, and stating quite flatfootedly that I know a little bit about hospital financial operations from personal contact over 18 years, I can come to but one conclusion, namely that the province of Quebec is bankrupt. There is no other possible way to explain the actions of that province in refusing to meet the needs of the hospitals of Quebec as outlined by individual hospitals to the Quebec hospital insurance commission once a year in their annual proposed budgets.
To bear out my statement that the hospitals of Montreal and throughout Quebec are being deliberately starved by the province of Quebec hospital insurance commission I would like to read from page 24 of the annual report of Mr. Eliot S. Frosst, the president. He is writing about the year ending December 31, 1966 and states:
The year just past has been one of the most trying and difficult years in the history of the hospital. Lack of space-badly congested areas, combined with what has been a constant struggle to meet our financial commitments have produced these conditions. Neither of these conditions is new-but last year at this time we had hoped that before another year had elapsed we would be able to report that ... a better understanding of our financial needs had been reached with the province. Unfortunately we are no further ahead than we were a year ago.
Although our treasurer, Mr. Lennox, will report on our financial position, I think that after six years of operation under the Quebec Hospital Insurance Service a few words on my part seem necessary. We are not unmindful of the problems confronting the governement in the operation and financing of the Quebec hospital insurance plan. However, our statements show that the hospital does not have the necessary working capital to finance the annual shortfall between our operating expenses and the budget approved by Q.H.I.S. For the years 1961-64, Q.H.I.S. has paid the hospital, based on final audits, our actual shareable costs, less only about 3.5 per cent. The hospital can finance this reduction from donations it receives from a generous public. The hospital is, however, in no position to finance the shortfall for approximately two years until the audit is completed. The budgets for the last two years have been cut by approximately 25 per cent. It is our duty to practice economies wherever possible and a determined effort is being made towards this end.
However, the hospital cannot possibly cut its expenses by 25 per cent and still maintain the standard of patient care that has made it one of the leading pediatric teaching hospitals on the North American continent.
It is the general practice throughout the ten provinces which are participating in this hospital scheme, in which the federal government participates, that toward the end of
IMr. Cowan.]
each fiscal year they submit a budget for the coming year. These budgets are approved and accepted in four to six weeks by the provincial commission. During the year for which the budget has been submitted checks are sent out semi-monthly to cover expenses that have already been approved. I know of no province in the Dominion of Canada, except the province of Quebec, where hospitals are complaining about a delay in receiving moneys from the department of health. This involves money received from the federal department of health, representing our shared costs of provincial health schemes.
The language used by Douglas Lennox, chartered accountant and honorary treasurer of the hospital, in the same report, bears out Mr. Frosst.
In my report last year-
That was for 1965.
-I outlined the difficulties involved in financing the operations of the hospital during 1965. The report of the president this year has informed you that these difficulties have not only continued during 1966, but have increased to such an extent that the financial position of the hospital is now extremely grave-
In 1966 our operating expenditures exceeded revenue by $2,521,905. Of this amount we consider that $2,075,391 should be reimbursed by Quebec hospital insurance service and a claim has therefore been lodged for this amount. Together with the balance of similar claims relating to prior years, the total amount which we believe should be reimbursed by the service amounted at the end of the 1966 fiscal year to $3,066,411. The corresponding amount at the end of 1965 was $2,416,731.

Mr. Speaker, the system between ourselves and the Quebec government in respect of hospital insurance is as follows. Early in the year the province sends us an estimate of their approved costs for the year. This estimate is reviewed by us and may be amended if we consider it unreasonable. We calculate the normal hospital insurance contribution to Quebec based on the amended estimate. This estimate is sent to the Department of Finance, with a copy to the Quebec hospital insurance authorities. On receipt of our estimates, the Department of Finance estimates the value of 14 points of personal income tax to Quebec, deducts this estimate from our total estimated contribution to Quebec under hospital insurance and makes monthly payments for the balance over the fiscal year.
If during the fiscal year the estimate of the hospital insurance contribution is changed, or the estimate of the value of the 14 income tax points, the new amount owing to Quebec is calculated and the payments are spread evenly over the balance of the fiscal year. After the close of the fiscal year the final contribution for the year under hospital insurance is determined in the usual way by the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the final value of 14 income tax points is determined by the Department of Finance. The final amount payable to Quebec for the year is then calculated by the Department of Finance and the current payments are adjusted upward or downward to compensate for this final adjustment.
We have been assured by some Quebec hospitals and by the Quebec hospital insurance service that regular semi-monthly payment cheques, based on one twentyfourth of the approved budgets, are being sent out to the hospitals on a regular basis. We receive monthly reports from Quebec on their payments to hospitals, and a review of these reports for 1967 indicates that the actual payments being made to the hospitals are almost identical with the estimates on which the federal contribution was calculated.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
We wish to confirm that we have had verbal assurance from the Quebec provincial authorities that bi-monthly payments representing one twentyfourth of the original approved budget are made regularly to the Montreal Children's Hospital. We also have
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion verbal assurance from the authorities of the Montreal Children's Hospital that such payments are received regularly. The monthly reports received from Quebec on their payments to hospitals are global reports not showing payments made to individual hospitals.
It would appear that the root of the problem is in two areas: first, the actual hospital costs are running in excess of the approved budgets, and second, final settlements for previous years between the Quebec hospital insurance service and each individual hospital are subject to long delays because of the difficulties encountered in verifying the actual hospital costs and assessing the reasonableness of over-expenditures in excess of approved budgets.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 23 of this year the food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare issued proposed changes which cover the addition of vitamin and mineral nutrients to drugs. In other words, these changes deal with vitamin supplements, treating them as drugs and not as food supplements. Yet, as Mr. S. A. Smith, the president of the Canadian Health Food Dealers Association has stated in a round robin letter:
Vitamins and minerals, with a couple of exceptions, are harmless, nontoxic food nutrients and should be freely available to the public without being told to consult a physician before using. Those with toxic effects should be regulated.
It is a truism that what is one man's meat can well be another man's poison, but those who take vitamin supplements usually find the level which best suits them and, just as those who eat bread, do not gorge incessantly or indiscriminately.
The minister himself, in a round robin letter of September 27, which begins "Dear Sir or Madam"-I wish he would make up his mind-dealt with the avalanche of protests which have come to his office in connection with these regulations. He said in part:
It is true that the amounts of vitamins presently used in vitamin preparations have not been shown to be toxic.
Toxics are being sold, but without anywhere near the precautions surrounding the sale of vitamins. I refer of course to cigarettes. It would make more sense to me if the
November 20, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Department of National Health and Welfare had taken some steps to prevent me from the folly of smoking cigarettes rather than putting certain conditions on the use of vitamin supplements, if I should ever take them up.
Since I have a number of questions, it would be unfair to expect the parliamentary secretary to answer all or many of them, and I think that this matter could be considered by the committee on health and welfare. They are as follows: first, what evil or what problem was being overcome by this decision of the food and drug directorate? Second, what scientific studies were made to justify bringing in these regulations? Third, who was consulted? Fourth, were requests made for such action and, if so, who made them? Fifth, will the effect not be to increase costs for those who take the higher doses of vitamin supplements, especially the older and poorer people?
I hold no brief in this matter. As I said, I do not take vitamin supplements myself, although inadvertently some of them might be slipped into some of the things I do take. I have always admired the work of the food and drug directorate, but has it gone too far, as is suggested by some of the criticisms that have come into the minister's department? I am puzzled, sir, and so are thousands of other Canadians. I hope that the minister, the parliamentary secretary, or the department will provide answers, if not now then before the committee on health and welfare.

I ask the indulgence of Mr. Speaker and his permission to conclude my remarks because if they are taken in part they might be misinterpreted. I do agree with the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), and perhaps he does need some vitamins, but he is not aware of it. If I may be permitted to ask your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I should like some extra time, if I need it, in order to conclude my remarks.
As part of its continuing program to protect Canadian consumers against health hazard and fraud in the advertising and sale of drugs, the food and drug directorate of my department recently proposed certain amendments in the regulations pertaining to vitamins and minerals in drugs. These proposals
[Mr. McCleave.1
were circulated to drug manufacturers as trade information letter No. 284, dated May 23, 1967. These manufacturers were requested to submit comments not later than October 1, 1967. Numerous constructive suggestions on these proposals have been received. I understand that the Canadian Health Food Dealers Association has played a major role in eliciting comments from individual consumers, many of which have been received by members of this house and by officials of my department as signed form letters. Since there appears to have been considerable misunderstanding by some consumers in regard both to the intent and effect of the proposed regulations, I should like to make a statement on this matter.
Available evidence indicates that most Canadians are well fed, and will not benefit from use of dietary supplements containing vitamins and minerals. Nutrition authorities agree that the best way to assure nutritional health is to eat well balanced meals. I certainly have, sir. However, since some individuals feel that they benefit from dietary supplements, provision is made for their sale in the food and drug regulations.
The present regulations, enacted a number of years ago, set minimum and maximum limits on the amount of vitamins in preparations which can be advertised to the general public. They were enacted under authority of section 9(1) of the Food and Drugs Act to prevent the consumer being misled as to the value, merit and safety of products containing either insignificant or excessive amounts of nutrients. Preparations which contain vitamins at levels above the specified amounts cannot be advertised to the general public and must, at the present time, carry on both the inner and outer labels the statement, "Note: for therapeutic use only". This cautionary statement is intended to inform consumers that high potency vitamin products should not be used to supplement the ordinary diet but are intended for treatment of vitamins deficiency states. Because of their nature, such conditions should be treated under the direction of a qualified physician.
It has become evident that the levels of vitamins and minerals presently permitted in products which can be advertised to the general public provide considerably more than the daily intakes required.
